title: Statement ordering and output tracing in R
breadcrumb: Module 9 · R Programming · Statement ordering and output tracing
objectives: Trace assignments and expressions in source order.
Follow conditional and loop control flow.
Distinguish printed output from returned values.
Compute final values using updated bindings.

traps: R normally evaluates statements in source order.
A later assignment changes the value used by later expressions.
Only the selected if/else branch executes.
break exits the nearest loop; next skips the current iteration.
Assignment does not automatically print a value.
Printed output and a function's returned value are different.

sheet: Read the snippet from top to bottom.
Record initial values before executing statements.
Apply each assignment immediately; later expressions use updated values.
Evaluate the if condition and follow only the selected branch.
Trace loops iteration by iteration; next skips and break exits.
print() displays an object; it does not reassign the name.
Check the final expression when asked for a function's return value.
For nested loops, identify which loop each break or next affects.
shortcuts: Create one row per statement or loop iteration.

howto: Use a trace table. Write initial bindings, process statements in source order, evaluate each condition, record loop iterations, and distinguish displayed output from the value returned by a function.

scenes.title: Read code as an ordered sequence
body: R normally evaluates expressions in source order. A later statement uses the values established by earlier assignments.
An assignment updates a name-to-value binding. It does not automatically print the assigned value.
A reliable output trace starts with initial values and records every change.

refresh: An assignment such as x <- 4 creates or updates the binding named x. A later expression that refers to x uses the latest value established by executed statements.
For output questions, keep a small state table. Record the value after every assignment rather than trying to remember several updates mentally; this prevents accidentally using an old value.

items.ask: What is the default order of statement evaluation?
items.recall: Statements normally execute in source order.
refresh: R normally evaluates expressions in the order they appear. A statement later in the same execution path sees the effects of earlier assignments and function calls.
Control-flow statements can change which lines execute, but they do not change the basic rule that the selected sequence is followed in order. Mark skipped and unselected lines explicitly.

items.ask: What is the difference between break and next?
items.recall: break exits the nearest loop; next skips the current iteration.
refresh: break terminates the nearest enclosing loop immediately. next skips the remaining statements in the current iteration and proceeds to the next iteration, if one remains.
For a loop trace, check the location of break or next before applying later statements in that iteration. This is especially important when an accumulator update appears after the control statement.

scenes.title: Follow the state changes
body: For x <- 2; x <- x+3; x*2, the second statement changes x to 5 and the final expression is 10.
Never use an old value after a later assignment has updated the binding.

scenario.title: An analyst updates a threshold
body: An analyst begins with threshold=10, changes it to threshold+5, then compares a score with the updated threshold.
The final comparison must use 15, not the original 10.

A reliable trace records the value of every variable after each executed statement and notes the exact iteration at which a branch or loop-control command is reached. Lines that are skipped must not be included in the final calculation. The final expression is evaluated only after all earlier updates on the executed path have been applied.

ask.q: Does an else branch execute when the if condition is TRUE?

scenes.title: Guided trace
scenes.problem: x <- 1; if(x>0) x <- x+4 else x <- x-4; x.
scenes.check: The condition is TRUE; x becomes 5.

ask.q: What changes if the condition is FALSE?

solution.why: Record the value before executing the conditional.

solution.say: Evaluate the condition and follow its branch.
solution.math: x > 0 is TRUE, so x becomes 1 + 4 = 5.
solution.why: Only the selected if branch executes.

solution.math: The final value of x is 5.
solution.why: The last expression uses the updated binding.

scenes.title: Loop trace drill
scenes.problem: x <- 1; for(i in 1:5){if(i==3) break; x <- x+i}; x.
hints: At i=3, break exits before the addition.
scenes.check: Only i=1 and i=2 update x.

scenario.teaser: Stop a calculation at a threshold
scenario.title: A quality-control loop
body: An analyst adds successive values to an accumulator but stops when the loop reaches a specified iteration.
The break statement exits before the update on that iteration, so the final accumulator includes only earlier additions.

A reliable trace records the value of every variable after each executed statement and notes the exact iteration at which a branch or loop-control command is reached. Lines that are skipped must not be included in the final calculation. The final expression is evaluated only after all earlier updates on the executed path have been applied.
scenario.q: Does the iteration that triggers break update the accumulator?
scenario.answer: No; break exits before the later update statement.

solution.math: i = 1 gives x = 2; i = 2 gives x = 4.
solution.why: Each iteration adds i to the current accumulator.

solution.math: At i = 3, the break statement executes.
solution.why: break exits the nearest loop before the following addition.
No update occurs for i=3 or for later iterations after the loop exits.

scenes.title: The output-tracing checklist
body: Read the snippet from top to bottom and write initial values.
Apply assignments in order; later expressions use updated bindings.
Evaluate if conditions and follow only the selected branch.
Trace loops iteration by iteration; apply next and break exactly where encountered.
Distinguish printed output, intermediate values and a function's returned value.
